content: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. This mutation disrupts the normal regulation of salt and water movement across cell membranes. In the liver, this abnormality results in focal biliary fibrosis, which can progress to portal hypertension and, in some cases, end-stage liver disease. While this condition may initially be asymptomatic, it can lead to complications such as splenomegaly, hypersplenism, the formation of varices, variceal bleeding, and ascites. These complications negatively affect the overall nutritional status and respiratory function of individuals with cystic fibrosis. Once significant portal hypertension develops, the prognosis becomes poor. Currently, the role and outcomes of various interventions for managing advanced liver disease, specifically non-malignant end-stage liver disease, in individuals with cystic fibrosis remain unclear. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of available treatment options for preventing and managing advanced liver disease in both children and adults with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a thorough search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, journal handsearching, and conference abstract books. The last search of this register was performed on November 19, 2019. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles and reviews, as well as online trial registries, were searched, with the last search conducted on January 1, 2020. The review sought to include any published or unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials that addressed advanced liver disease in cystic fibrosis, specifically cases involving cirrhosis, liver failure, portal hypertension, or variceal bleeding. However, after independently screening titles and abstracts, the authors found no eligible trials for inclusion in the review. The main finding of this review is that no published randomized controlled trials were identified that met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, the authors concluded that there is a critical need to conduct randomized controlled trials to establish evidence-based interventions for preventing and managing advanced liver disease in both children and adults with cystic fibrosis.
